entries.narration: Python is a general-purpose programming language, and before we write a single line of it, it is worth knowing what kind of language it is, because those five words on the left of the screen explain almost everything you will meet in this course. It is high-level: you describe what you want done, and Python takes care of how the machine does it, so you never manage memory addresses or registers. It is interpreted: you write a file and run it, with no separate compile step to wait for, which is why trying an idea in Python takes seconds. It is dynamically typed: a value knows its own type, a number or a piece of text, but a name does not, so the same name can point at different kinds of value over time. It is garbage-collected: when nothing uses a value any more, Python reclaims the memory for you. And it is multi-paradigm: you can write a ten-line script, a set of small functions, or a system built from objects, and all three are ordinary Python. Now look to the right. The same language turns up in very different jobs. Web sites and the services behind them, with Django, Flask and FastAPI. Data analysis in notebooks, with pandas, NumPy and Jupyter. Machine learning, where PyTorch, TensorFlow and scikit-learn are written to be driven from Python. Data engineering, where Airflow schedules pipelines, PySpark drives Spark, and DuckDB queries files directly. Infrastructure tools like Ansible, the cloud providers' own SDKs, and countless command-line tools. And the everyday automation of moving files, filling spreadsheets and reading web pages. This course stays in one of these worlds, data engineering, and builds a real pipeline from an empty folder. But everything you learn transfers to the others, because it is all the same language. Next, where that language came from.

Python is older than most people expect. In December 1989, Guido van Rossum, a programmer at the CWI research institute in Amsterdam, started writing a new language over the holidays. He had a specific gap in mind. Guido had worked on ABC, a language designed to be easy to read and teach, but ABC was closed: you could not extend it or connect it to the outside world. And on Amoeba, the operating system project he was working on, he kept needing something in between the two tools he had. Shell scripts were quick to write but too weak for real programs. C was powerful, but slow to write and to debug. Python was built to sit in that gap: as readable as ABC, but open, extensible, and able to talk to the operating system. He named it after the comedy series Monty Python's Flying Circus, not the snake. The first public version, 0.9.0, appeared in February 1991, and it already had classes, exceptions, functions, and the lists, dictionaries and strings you will use in almost every program in this course. Version 1.0 followed in January 1994. The second era began in October 2000 with Python 2.0, which brought list comprehensions, a compact way of building lists that you will meet in the processing course, and a garbage collector that could clean up objects referring to each other. In 2001 the Python Software Foundation was formed to own the language, so it no longer depended on one company or one person. Then, in December 2008, came the decision that defines modern Python. Python 3.0 deliberately broke compatibility with Python 2, to fix mistakes that could not be fixed any other way. The table on the right shows the ones you would notice. Print became a function. Dividing seven by two gives three and a half instead of quietly throwing away the half. Text became Unicode by default, so names in any language just work. The two versions lived side by side for over a decade, until Python 2 reached its end of life in January 2020. Since then, Python 3 has moved quickly. Guido stepped down as the language's lead in 2018, and an elected Steering Council took over. Since 2020 a new version has shipped every October. Python 3.11 made the interpreter about twenty five percent faster on average. Python 3.13 added an experimental build without the global interpreter lock, and 3.14 made that build officially supported. That lock, and what removing it means, is part of the next course.

Most languages have a style guide. Python has a philosophy, and it ships inside the language. Type python, dash c, import this, and Python prints nineteen short lines called the Zen of Python, written by Tim Peters, one of the language's early core developers. You do not need to memorise them, but three ideas run through all of them, and they will shape every piece of code in this course. The first is that readability counts. Code is read far more often than it is written, so Python is designed to be read. Look at the small file on the right. There are no braces and no end markers. The indentation itself is the structure: the line that prints is indented under the if, which is indented under the for, and that is exactly how Python runs it. What you see is what runs. The second idea is batteries included. Python ships with a large standard library, so a lot of real work needs nothing installed at all. The modules on screen are the ones our pipeline will use: csv and json to read the shop's files, sqlite3 to load a database, pathlib to find files, datetime for dates, decimal for money, statistics for summaries, and logging to record what happened. Every one of them comes with Python. The third idea is in the line about having one obvious way to do it, and in how the language changes. Every change to Python is written up as a PEP, a Python Enhancement Proposal, discussed in public, and accepted or rejected by the elected Steering Council. Beyond the standard library, the Python Package Index holds hundreds of thousands of packages written by the community. In this course we stay with the standard library for the pipeline itself, and add a few tools only when we start testing and checking it. Next, an honest look at what Python is good at, and what it is not.

No language is the right choice for everything, and knowing where Python fits will make you a better engineer than pretending it fits everywhere. The table on the left is the honest version. Python is strong for automation and for gluing systems together, because the code is short and the standard library covers so much. It is strong for data analysis and machine learning. It is strong for data pipelines, which is what we are building. For web back ends it is good, and frameworks like Django and FastAPI run large sites, though at very large scale teams sometimes reach for Go or Java. And it is a weak choice for mobile apps, and not a native choice in the browser, where Kotlin, Swift and JavaScript own the platforms. The interesting row is the slow one, and the terminal on the right shows why. Both commands add up the same million numbers. The first does it with an ordinary Python loop, one number at a time. The second calls the built-in sum function. On the machine this course was made on, the loop took about eighteen milliseconds, and sum took about four, close to five times faster, for exactly the same answer. The numbers will differ on your machine, but the gap will not go away, and the reason is worth understanding now. A Python loop runs one bytecode instruction at a time, with the interpreter checking types as it goes. The built-in sum does the same work in compiled C. That is also the secret behind Python's strength in data and machine learning: NumPy, pandas and PyTorch keep their inner loops in C, C plus plus or on a GPU, and Python only directs them. So the rule is simple. Write the logic in Python, and let the heavy loops run in code that was built for speed. You will see that rule again when we make the pipeline fast. Next, the pipeline itself.

Everything in this course builds one real program: a data pipeline for a small coffee roastery. Every day, the roastery's online shop writes a file of the day's orders. On the left is one of those files, as it really looks. Each line is one order: an order number, the date, the customer, the product code, and how many bags. Look at the highlighted line. The quantity says three, written as a word, not a number. Real data always has lines like that, and a good pipeline has to deal with them without crashing and without quietly getting the totals wrong. The pipeline works in three stages, and data engineers call them E, T and L. Extract reads every day's file and checks every row, keeping the good ones and reporting the bad. Transform prices each line from the product catalogue and adds up the revenue for each product. Load writes the results somewhere useful: a SQLite database that keeps every priced line, and a daily report. On the right is the report this exact file produces, from a real run. Three bags of the Ethiopian coffee, one of the Brazilian, one of the Colombian, seventy one dollars and fifty cents in total, and one order rejected, with the reason, so somebody can fix it. The small numbers on each stage are the courses that build it. Extract is course six. Transform is courses five and seven. Load is course eight. And the courses along the bottom are the ones around the pipeline: how Python runs, setting up the project, holding the data in memory, and then, once the pipeline works, structuring it, testing it, making it fast and shipping it as a job that runs on a schedule. From course three onwards, every lesson shows you the project the way a developer sees it, with the files on the left, the code in the middle, and the terminal showing exactly what happens when it runs. Next course: what actually happens when you run a Python file.

When you type python and the name of a file, it feels as if Python simply reads your code and does it. In fact your code goes through six stages before anything appears on the screen, and this frame follows one line, total equals price times quantity, through all of them. First, Python reads the file. To Python it is only text at this point. Second, the tokenizer splits that text into words, which Python calls tokens. The real output in the second panel shows the line becoming five tokens: a name, an equals sign, another name, a star, and a third name. Third, the parser checks that those tokens form valid Python, and builds a tree describing what the line means: an assignment, whose value is a multiplication, whose left side is the name price and whose right side is the name quantity. If you ever get a SyntaxError, this is the stage that raised it, before a single line of your program ran. Fourth, the compiler turns the tree into bytecode: small, simple instructions for a machine that does not physically exist. The bottom row shows the four instructions this line becomes: load price, load quantity, multiply, store the result as total. Fifth, the Python virtual machine runs those instructions in a loop: fetch the next one, do it, repeat. And sixth, the result you asked for appears: nineteen point zero. Two things are worth holding on to. Python is not running your text directly; it runs bytecode compiled from it, every time. And the machine that runs it is a program too, written in C, called CPython, which is the Python you installed. The rest of this course opens each stage up. Next, the bytecode itself, and where Python keeps it.

Compiling every file on every run would waste time, so Python keeps the bytecode it compiles for modules you import. Look at the project on the left. Main dot py imports a function from pricing dot py. After one run, a new folder has appeared: double underscore pycache. Inside it is pricing dot cpython three thirteen dot pyc, the compiled bytecode of the pricing module. The name tells you which interpreter made it, so if you run the same project with a different Python version, each version keeps its own cache instead of reading the wrong one. On the right is what that file holds for the line total function, shown with the dis module, Python's disassembler. Four instructions: resume, load both arguments, multiply, and return. Notice that main dot py has no pyc file. The script you run directly is compiled fresh every time and never cached; only modules you import are. The rules are short, and they are in the list. An imported module is compiled once and the bytecode is saved. The cache records the source file's modification time and size, so the next time you import it, Python checks whether the source has changed: if it has, it compiles again; if not, it loads the saved bytecode and skips the work. You never need to manage this folder yourself, and it is safe to delete, because Python rebuilds it. It also belongs in your gitignore file, since it is generated, not written. In a small project you will not notice the time saved. In a large one, with hundreds of modules imported at start-up, the cache is the difference between starting instantly and starting slowly. Next, what the virtual machine does with those instructions.

Python's virtual machine is a stack machine, and once you see what that means, bytecode stops looking mysterious. Picture a stack of plates. You can put a plate on top, and you can take the top plate off, and that is all. The machine keeps a stack like that for values, and almost every instruction either pushes something onto it, or pops something off it, or both. The table follows the four instructions of our line, step by step. Step one, load name price: Python looks up the name price, finds nine point five, and pushes it. The stack now holds one value. Step two, load name quantity: two goes on top, so the stack holds nine point five and two. Step three, binary op multiply: it pops the top two values, multiplies them, and pushes the single result, nineteen point zero. Step four, store name total: it pops that result and binds the name total to it, leaving the stack empty, exactly as it started. Every expression you will ever write works this way. A longer calculation simply means more loads and more operations, and the order of the instructions is the order Python evaluates your expression in, which is how operator precedence becomes real. There are no registers to manage and no addresses: everything passes through the stack, which is what makes the bytecode so compact and so easy for the interpreter to run. It is also part of why pure Python loops are slower than C: each of these small steps is a separate trip around the evaluation loop. Next, what happens to this stack when one function calls another.

A program is mostly functions calling other functions, and Python keeps track of that with a second stack, the call stack. Every time you call a function, Python creates a frame: a small record holding that function's own names and values, and the place to return to when it finishes. The new frame goes on top. When the function returns, its frame is removed, and the function underneath carries on exactly where it stopped. The file in the editor has three levels: the script itself calls order total, which calls line total. Inside line total, line seven asks Python to list the frames that exist at that moment, and the terminal shows the answer: line total, then order total, then module, which is Python's name for the script itself. Newest first. On the right is that same moment drawn as a stack. At the top, line total is running, and its frame holds just two names: the product code and the quantity. Underneath, order total is paused, waiting for line total to return. Its frame has its own names, including total, which is still zero, because the first line has not been added yet. At the bottom is the module's frame, holding the global names: the price table and the two functions. Two consequences matter for the rest of the course. Each call gets its own frame, so two functions can use the same name, like quantity, without interfering. And when something goes wrong deep inside a call, Python can tell you exactly how you got there, by reading this stack from top to bottom. That is what a traceback is, and we will read one at the end of this course. Next, what a name actually is.

Here is the most important idea in this course, and the one that surprises people coming from other languages. In Python, a variable is not a box that holds a value. It is a name, attached to an object. Look at the second line of the file. Same equals order. It is tempting to read that as copying the list. It does not copy anything. It takes the name same and attaches it to the object that order already refers to. There is still exactly one list. Then the third line appends a third coffee to it through the name same, and the terminal shows the result: printing order shows three items, because order and same are two names for the same list. Python confirms it two ways: same is order is true, and the two identities are equal. The diagram on the right shows the real arrangement. Names live in a namespace, which is simply a dictionary from names to objects; at the top level of a script it is called the global namespace, and every function call gets a fresh one of its own, in its frame. Objects live separately, on the heap, and a name only ever points at one. So assignment never copies. It binds a name. If you actually want a second, independent list, you have to ask for one, with a copy, and you will see how in the course on holding data. Keep this picture in mind whenever a value seems to change behind your back: the question to ask is how many names point at that object. Next, the objects themselves.

Every object in Python has exactly three things: an identity, a type, and a value, and knowing which one you are asking about prevents a whole class of bugs. In this file, a and b are two lists built separately with the same contents. The terminal shows what Python thinks of them. A equals equals b is true: double equals compares values, and both lists hold the same two products. But a is b is false: is compares identity, and these are two different objects. The third line prints their identities with the id function. In CPython the identity is the object's address in memory, which is why the numbers are large, and why you will see different numbers every time you run it. Only the comparison matters, never the number itself. The fourth line asks for types: a is a list, and len of a is an int. The type decides what an object can do; a list can be appended to, an int can be added. On the right, the two objects sit on the heap side by side: different identities, the same type, equal values. So the rule is simple. Use double equals to ask whether two things have the same value, which is what you want almost every time. Use is only to ask whether two names point at the very same object, and in everyday code that mostly means checking for None, as in x is None. Mixing them up is a classic bug: two lists can be equal without being the same object, and changing one then leaves the other untouched. Next, how long an object lives, and who decides when it goes.

Python reclaims memory for you, and the main way it does it is surprisingly simple. Every object keeps a count of how many references point at it. When the count drops to zero, nothing can reach the object any more, and CPython frees it immediately. This file watches the count change. Python's sys module has a function, getrefcount, that reports it, with one catch: the act of passing the object to the function adds a temporary reference, so it always reports one more than you might expect. The table on the right shows both numbers. After order is created, there is one real reference and getrefcount says two. Binding a second name, alias, makes it two real references and three reported. Deleting alias brings it back down. Del does not destroy the object, by the way. It removes a name, and the count goes down with it. Reference counting has one blind spot: a cycle. The last lines of the file build a dictionary that contains itself. When its name is deleted, the dictionary still refers to itself, so its count can never reach zero, and counting alone would keep it forever. For that, CPython has a second mechanism, the cycle collector, which periodically looks for groups of objects that only refer to each other. Calling gc dot collect runs it now, and it reports that it freed one object: our self-referencing dictionary. In practice you will almost never call it yourself; it runs automatically. What you should take away is the model: an object lives as long as something refers to it, and the pipeline we build will lean on that when it processes a month of orders without holding them all in memory. Next, the lock that has shaped Python's history.

Your computer almost certainly has several processor cores, so it is natural to expect that two threads would do twice the work in the same time. In the default build of CPython, for code that is busy computing, they do not, and this file shows it. It counts down from twenty million twice, first one count after the other, then on two threads at the same time. The terminal shows one run on the machine this course was made on: about a second either way. Run it a few times and the two numbers trade places by a tenth of a second or so, which is just noise; what never happens is two threads finishing in half the time. The reason is the global interpreter lock, the GIL. In the default build, a thread must hold this one lock to run Python bytecode, so only one thread runs bytecode at any moment, however many cores you have. The lock made CPython's memory management simple and safe, and it is why reference counting, from the last section, never needs extra locks. It does not make threads useless. A thread that is waiting, for a file, a database or the network, releases the lock while it waits, so threads that mostly wait still overlap very well, and you will use exactly that when the pipeline reads many sources at once. Things are changing. Python 3.13 introduced an experimental free-threaded build with no GIL, and Python 3.14 made it officially supported. It is a separate interpreter, called python three fourteen t, where threads really do run bytecode on separate cores at the same time. This machine only has the default build, so that behaviour is described here, not measured. When we make the pipeline fast, we will choose between threads, processes and asyncio with this in mind. Next, the last piece: reading an error.

Every Python programmer spends a lot of time reading tracebacks, and most beginners read them in the wrong order. A traceback is the call stack from earlier in this course, printed at the moment something went wrong. In this file, the order contains a product code, K E N two fifty, that is not in the price table, and the terminal shows what happens. The rule is: read it from the bottom up. The last line is what went wrong. KeyError, KEN two fifty: Python looked up that key in a dictionary and it was not there. Very often that line alone tells you the fix. The line above it is where it happened: line five, in line total, the newest frame, which was running when the error was raised, with the exact expression underlined. Above that is who called it: line eleven, in order total. And at the top is where the whole run started: line fifteen, in the module. The highlighted lines in the editor are those same three places, and the table below lays out the reading order. Reading from the top first sends you to the line where the program started, which is almost never where the problem is. Two more things to notice. The little carets and tildes under each line point at the exact part of the expression that failed, which matters when one line does several things. And nothing after the error ran: the total was never printed. Later in the course the pipeline will catch exactly this kind of error, so that one bad product code is reported instead of stopping a whole day's run. That completes the picture of how Python runs your code. In the next course, we start the project.
